title: How the FBR POS Invoicing System Works in Pakistan
metaDescription: A plain-English walkthrough of how the FBR POS invoicing system works in Pakistan — from a sale, to IRIS submission, to the QR code a customer can verify.
content:
The system in one sentence

The FBR POS invoicing system is the real-time link between a Pakistani business's point of sale and the Federal Board of Revenue: every sale is reported to FBR IRIS as it happens, and the customer receives a QR-coded invoice they can verify. Understanding how it works end to end makes the difference between trusting your receipts and actually being compliant — because the two are not always the same thing.

What happens at the moment of sale

When a cashier finalises a bill, several things happen in under a second:

  1. The POS builds the invoice — items, amounts, and tax.
  2. It submits to FBR IRIS over the IRIS API using your registered credentials.
  3. IRIS validates and responds with a unique invoice reference number.
  4. The POS encodes that reference into a QR code.
  5. The receipt prints with the QR — on paper, or sent by WhatsApp or SMS.

Each step has to succeed for the invoice to be real. If the submission fails but the receipt still prints, you have a piece of paper that proves nothing.

Why the QR code is the whole point

The QR encodes the reference IRIS issued, so a customer — or an FBR inspector — can scan it and see the verified record on the FBR portal. A QR that does not resolve to a real IRIS record is just an image. This is why the printed receipt is not proof of compliance; the IRIS record is.

Where the system depends on good engineering

Behind the scenes, the invoicing system relies on a few technical details that decide whether it stays reliable: authentication tokens that expire roughly hourly and must refresh proactively, an offline queue that holds sales during outages and submits them with their original timestamps, and retry logic for when IRIS rate-limits a busy business. A POS that handles these quietly keeps invoicing valid; one that does not produces silent failures.

A real example

A shop owner in Faisalabad assumed that because receipts were printing, everything was fine. In fact a token problem meant half a day's invoices never reached IRIS — the QR codes pointed at nothing. The invoicing system was 'working' at the counter and failing at FBR, the exact gap this design can hide if you do not verify.

Making the system work for you

Treat the IRIS dashboard as the source of truth, verify a few QR codes regularly, and reconcile monthly. For the verification step see how to generate valid FBR QR invoices, and if invoices stop reaching IRIS, the guide to common FBR POS issues explains why.

faqs.question: What is the FBR POS invoicing system?
faqs.answer: It is the real-time process by which a registered business reports each sale to FBR IRIS and issues a QR-coded invoice. The system links your point of sale to FBR so every transaction is recorded as it happens.

faqs.question: Does the customer get a normal receipt?
faqs.answer: Yes — it looks like a normal receipt but carries a QR code. Scanning it lets anyone confirm on the FBR portal that the sale was genuinely reported, which is the proof of compliance.

faqs.question: What makes an invoice 'valid' under this system?
faqs.answer: That it was accepted by IRIS and the QR encodes the reference IRIS returned. A locally printed receipt with no matching IRIS record is not a valid FBR invoice, even if it looks the part.

faqs.question: Is the whole thing automatic?
faqs.answer: Once configured, yes. The POS submits, IRIS validates and returns a reference, the POS prints the QR — all in the moment of sale, with no manual steps for staff.
